$schema.description: The JSON Schema of this file, for the editor (such as "./node_modules/svg-diagram/schema/spec.schema.json"). The CLIs ignore it.

lang.description: The language of the words the figure writes by itself (legends, headings such as 'Today'): ja (default) or en. Write your own text in the same language.

title.description: The accessible name of the figure. Drawn above it only with showTitle.
title.patternErrorMessage: Write plain text on one line: not blank, no line break or other control character.

showTitle.description: true: draw the title above the figure.

desc.description: A one-sentence description for screen readers.
desc.patternErrorMessage: Write plain text on one line: not blank, no line break or other control character.

sourceLine.description: Where the content comes from, printed under the figure.
sourceLine.patternErrorMessage: Write plain text on one line: not blank, no line break or other control character.

width.description: The width the figure is laid out at, in px (320 to 940, default 940): narrower makes boxes and tables wrap their text instead of the figure being shrunk later (a column of a slide). Text sizes do not change.

legend.description: 'auto' lists the notation used; false shows no legend.

width.description: The width of the canvas in px (default 1280).

height.description: The height of the canvas in px (default 720). With fit 'content', the most it may be.

minText.description: The smallest text in px (default 24). Every text, box and gap grows by minText / 14.

fit.description: 'content': the canvas is as tall as what it holds, up to height. Left out: always height tall.

canvas.description: A figure for a slide or a screen, shown at its own size (1920x1080 for a full HD slide), instead of a figure for a document (940px wide, shown in a text column). Text and boxes grow with minText, so a large canvas holds more only when minText stays small.

enumDescriptions: A flowchart: steps, decisions (a diamond holding the question) and start / end pills joined by arrows. Use for a process with branches or loops. Put Yes / No on the edges that leave a decision. When the decisions form one chain (the first yes decides), use decisionLadder: it is smaller and stays readable on a slide.

A decision ladder: yes/no questions stacked down the left; each yes goes right to its answer, each no goes down to the next question, and the last no ends in the final box. Use it when the decisions form ONE chain (the first question that is yes decides) and the figure must stay small and readable on a 16:9 slide; use flowchart when a no branches elsewhere or the flow loops. Anchors: q1..qN (questions), a1..aN (answers), otherwise (the final box); these ids are fixed, so a spec holds one decisionLadder (and no other part may use them).

A Theory of Constraints logic tree or another cause-and-effect diagram: boxes joined by arrows from cause to effect. Set `tree`: 'crt' for a Current Reality Tree (undesirable effects as role ude at the top, root causes as role root at the bottom), 'frt' for a Future Reality Tree (changes as role injection, results as role de, facts nobody controls as role precondition), 'prt' for a Prerequisite Tree, 'tt' for a Transition Tree, 'nbr' for a Negative Branch. Give a link an array as `from` when the causes are only sufficient together (AND). Saying `tree` also turns on the checks for that kind of tree.

A Theory of Constraints conflict cloud (evaporating cloud): the common objective A, the needs B and C, and the conflicting wants D and D2. B needs D, C needs D2. List the assumptions behind an arrow, and the injection that makes one false.
Porter's value chain: support activities across the top and primary activities along the bottom, with a margin arrow at the right end.

A mind map: one root with branches, for organising a topic. `layout` also gives an org chart ('org'), an indented list ('list'), a brace map ('brace'), a fishbone cause-and-effect chart ('fishbone') and a timeline ('timeline').

A matrix between two axes: 2x2 (or up to 4x4) cells, with items placed in a cell or at a coordinate, optionally as bubbles sized by a value. `preset` fills the axes and cells of a known framework: bcg (growth-share), ge (GE-McKinsey nine box), ansoff, nineBox (talent), impactEffort, risk (likelihood x impact), stakeholder (power x interest), positioning, eisenhower (urgent x important), actMatrix (ACT Matrix: five senses / inside x away / toward, with 気づいている自分 at the centre). The presets write their axes and cells in Japanese: with lang en, give x, y and cells (and centre) instead.
Process steps as arrow shapes in a row (or a column): a sequence with no branches, such as the phases of a project. `current` marks the step in progress.

Steps that repeat in a circle, such as PDCA: the last step leads back to the first. A word can sit in the centre. With links, the steps sit on a regular polygon joined pair by pair inside an optional named frame: the CBT five-part model.
Layers stacked from a wide base to a narrow top, such as a hierarchy of needs or of priorities. The first layer is the base, the last the top.
A state diagram: the states something goes through and the events that move it, such as an order or a ticket. `initial` draws the start dot; a final state has a double outline.
A Gantt chart: tasks as bars on a calendar, grouped by sections, with milestones, progress and arrows from the tasks a task waits for. Dates are YYYY-MM-DD; give `today` to draw the line of today.
A Venn diagram of two or three sets: what each has, and what they share. Overlaps are named by the names of their sets.
A funnel: stages that narrow, such as visits to orders. With values, the widths follow them and the rate between stages can be written.
A table: columns with headings and rows of text or numbers, such as a comparison of options. A row can be an object with a tone to stand out.

A customer journey map: the stages across the top, and rows (lanes) such as actions, touchpoints, feelings and issues. The lane with id 'emotion' holds a number from -2 (bad) to 2 (good) per stage and is drawn as a curve of feelings.
A RACI chart: who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each task. Each task has exactly one A and at least one R. A cell can hold several letters, such as A/R.

A why-why analysis (5 whys): the problem at the top, each answer to "why?" below the one it explains, root causes in a double frame, and what is done about each. Each answer should be a fact, not a person.

A swimlane: who does what over time. Lanes are the actors, columns are time. A step without `col` goes in the column after the step written before it, in any lane, so give `col` to line steps up; at most 8 columns. A label on a flow needs room: it fits on a flow that crosses both a lane and a column, but rarely between two touching steps.
A sequence diagram: messages between participants in time order. A step is a message (from, to, label), a self call (self, label), a note (note, over) or a divider (divider).

A bar chart: one bar per label, such as sales by month or votes by option. Values are 0 or more. dir v (columns) suits a few short labels or a time order; h (rows, the default) suits long labels or a ranking. Reference lines (a target, an average) need dir v.

A line chart: how values change over categories in order (months, years, stages), one line per series, each named at its end. Up to 6 series (plus ideal/plan lines, drawn dashed). Values can be negative. Each series has one value per category.

A stacked bar chart: each column is split into parts (the same series in every column), such as sales by product per quarter. The total is written on top. percent: true makes every column 100% and writes shares, for comparing make-up rather than size. Up to 6 series.

A waterfall chart: how a starting amount becomes an ending one through increases and decreases, such as last year's profit to this year's. The first step is the start (its level); every other step is a change (+ rises, - falls), unless its kind is subtotal or total, which shows the running level (its value may be left out).
A radar chart: several scores on axes around a centre, one polygon per series, such as skills of a person or features of products. 3 to 12 axes, 1 to 4 series, each with one value per axis.

A Pareto chart: causes or categories as bars from the largest down, with a cumulative-percent line, so the vital few that make up most (80%) stand out. Give the items in any order. top: N keeps the N largest and folds the rest into 'その他' (other).
A Sankey diagram: flows between stages, such as visitors to purchases or a budget to its uses. The height of a node and the thickness of a ribbon follow the value. Flows go one way: no cycles.

A treemap: shares of a whole as rectangles whose areas follow the values, such as sales by region and product. A cell with children is a group (its value is their sum); a cell too small for its name is drawn without it.
A heatmap: a table of numbers shaded by size, such as sales by month and store or a cohort retention. Every cell has a number; the darker, the larger.
A bubble chart: items placed by two measures (x, y) with a circle whose area is a third, such as products by growth, share and sales. Axes can have a dashed threshold line.
A tornado chart: how much a result moves when each input goes from its low to its high value, longest bar first, such as the sensitivity of a profit forecast. `base` is the result of the base case.
A strategy canvas (Blue Ocean): the factors of competition along the bottom and the level each company offers on each, one line per company. Levels run from min to max (default 0 to 5).

A business process in BPMN style: lanes (who) as rows, tasks, a start and an end event, and gateways (xor: one way, and: all ways in parallel, or: some ways) joined by flows. A flow out of a gateway carries its condition as a label; a dashed flow is a message between lanes. The columns follow the flow; a wide figure is narrowed to fit.

A UML class diagram: classes with attributes and methods, and relations. inherit and implement run from the child to the parent (triangle at the parent); compose and aggregate put the diamond on `from`, the whole; arrow is a directed association, depend a dashed dependency, assoc a plain line. Parents are placed above.

A PERT network (activity on node): tasks with a duration and the tasks that must finish first. The earliest and latest start and finish, the slack and the critical path (zero slack, drawn in red) are worked out. No task may depend on itself, directly or round a circle.

A time axis, in one of two forms. Date form: dates are 'YYYY', 'YYYY-MM' or 'YYYY-MM-DD'. Give any of now (today, always written out), the deadline the figure is about and marks (other dates); with both now and deadline the time left between them is written ('あと 1 年 3 か月'). from and to may be left out: the axis then runs from the first to the last date with a little padding. Number form: unit ('ms', '日' ...), from and to as numbers, lanes (rows), events (dots) and spans (bars, or a dimension line with dim).
A tree of boxes joined by lines, such as an organization, a breakdown of work (WBS) or a category hierarchy: the root at the top (or the left with dir right), each node with its children below it.

A dependency network: things (services, modules, teams) and typed arrows between them: depends, uses, blocks or relates. A node kind and each arrow type are named in a legend; a weight thickens the arrow.

A fault tree (FTA): the top event (the failure to prevent) at the top, a logic gate under each event (and, or, vote, inhibit) and its inputs below, down to basic events (circles) and undeveloped events (diamonds). An event with no gate needs a kind. `{ref: id}` repeats a basic event that feeds two gates. cutSets marks the events that alone cause the top event; quant works out its probability from every basic event's p.

A bow-tie diagram for a risk: the top event (the moment control is lost) in the middle under its hazard, the threats that cause it on the left with the preventive barriers between them and it, and the consequences on the right with the barriers that limit them. The figure is one row of boxes across: keep every label short (about 10 characters), and give at most two barriers per threat or consequence; one fits best.

An FMEA table (failure mode and effects analysis): for each item, how it can fail, the effect, the cause and the action, rated S (severity), O (occurrence) and D (detection) from 1 to 10. RPN = S x O x D is worked out and coloured against the threshold; `after` gives the ratings once the action is taken.

A Kepner-Tregoe IS / IS NOT table: for what, where, when and extent, what the problem IS and what it could be but IS NOT, the distinction between the two, and what changed around that distinction. dim is 'what', 'where', 'when', 'extent' or a heading of your own. At least one row needs a distinction.

A matrix diagram (L-shaped): options or causes as rows against criteria as columns, with ◎ (strong), ○, △ or × where they meet. With weights (the importance of each column), every row gets a score, Σ weight x value with ◎ 9, ○ 3, △ 1, × 0, and the best is marked.

A PDPC (process decision program chart): the steps from the start to the goal, what could go wrong on the way (role risk, a hexagon) and what to do then (role measure). The main path is solid; arrows into or out of a risk or a measure are dashed. A measure usually leads back to a step or on to the goal.

A relations diagram: the factors of a tangled problem and arrows from cause to effect, which may cross and go back. Each factor shows how many arrows leave and enter it; the factor with the most leaving arrows (2 or more) is marked as the key cause. `problem` names the result being analysed (red).

An affinity diagram (KJ method): cards of ideas or facts gathered into groups, each group named by a short sentence that says what its cards have in common. A group can be made of smaller groups (two levels below the top).

A causal loop diagram (systems thinking): variables joined by arrows marked + (they move the same way) or - (the opposite way); a delay is marked ||. Every closed loop is found and named R (reinforcing: an even number of -) or B (balancing: odd). Interventions are levers outside the loops, acting on a variable. layout 'ring' draws a figure that is exactly one loop as a circle.
Things done in order, with no dates: a row of boxes (title, body, tag) joined by arrows, numbered if wanted, one of them emphasised, and arrows back to earlier steps (loopBack) for rework.

Two sides compared in two framed columns, such as before and after, the usual view and the real cause, or plan A and plan B. A third frame under both (shared) can show what they have in common, joined to each side by an arrow.

Concentric circles: layers around a centre, such as stakeholders by distance, defence in depth or a core and its surroundings. labels: side writes each ring's name and description beside the circles. With sectors, the rings are cut into sectors and carry marks: the ACT Values Bullseye (life domains as sectors, how closely the week followed each value as the distance from the centre), a technology radar (Adopt / Trial / Assess / Hold as rings). A mark sits in a sector at a ring or at r (0 centre .. 1 edge); from (last time's ring or r) draws an arrow from where it was. layout: stack draws the same data as a column of boxes per sector, the innermost ring the top row.
Harvey balls: a table of options (columns) rated on criteria (rows) with circles filled from 0 (empty) to 4 (full), such as a comparison of products or vendors. A legend names the five levels.

A comparison table (比較表): options (columns) rated on criteria (rows), each cell a mark (◎ best, ○ good, △ fair, × poor) and the reason for it, set side by side so the marks read down a column and every rating says why. A cell that is not rated has the mark - (a dash). Use it to compare plans, products or vendors with reasons; for marks alone use matrix, for filled circles harvey.

A burndown chart: the work left at the end of each day of a sprint, against the ideal straight line from the total to 0. Days count from 0 (the start); give actual values only for the days reached so far.

A burnup chart: the work done by the end of each day climbing towards the scope, which can be one number or grow day by day. Days count from 0 (the start); give done values only for the days reached so far.

A Mekko (Marimekko) chart: the width of a column is its total and the height of a part its share, so each area is its share of the whole, such as market size by segment and the share of each company in it.
A butterfly chart: two groups compared row by row, bars running left and right from a shared middle column of labels, such as men and women by age or us and a competitor by criterion.

A combination chart: bars and lines over the same categories, the bars on the left axis and the lines on a right axis of their own, such as sales (bars) and profit margin in % (line). At most 3 bar and 3 line series.

A histogram (QC): the raw measurements are sorted into classes of a round width and drawn as touching bars. Give the specification limits (lsl, usl) to draw them and turn the classes outside red; the mean is drawn by default, the normal curve with normal: true.

A scatter diagram (QC): one point per pair of values, to see whether two things move together. Points with a group get a colour and a shape per group (at most 4 groups). regression: true draws the least-squares line and writes the correlation coefficient r.

A control chart (QC): the values in time order, the centre line and the 3-sigma limits worked out from the data; points outside the limits and runs of 7 are marked red. chart: x / mr / c take values; xbar / r take subgroups (2-10 measurements each); p / np / u take samples ({n inspected, d defective or defects}).

A check sheet (QC): the items (kinds of defect) down the side, the columns (days, machines, shifts) across, and the counts as tally marks with totals. Leave out counts for an empty sheet to fill in by hand.
Range bars: one bar per label from a low to a high value, such as the price range of each plan, an estimate range or a minimum and maximum. Values are 0 or more.

A box plot: the spread of the raw values of each group, the box from the first to the third quartile with the median, whiskers to 1.5 IQR and the values beyond as rings. Compares groups such as branches, lines or months.

A quality function deployment (QFD, house of quality without the roof): customer demands as rows, each with its importance, against quality characteristics as columns, with ◎ (strong, 9), ○ (3) or △ (1) where a characteristic serves a demand. Each column gets a score, Σ importance x value, and its share in percent; the top characteristic is marked.

A why-why analysis as a table: the problem in the first column, then each chain of answers to "why?" across a row (why 1, why 2, ...), its root cause and what is done about it. Use it when the chains do not branch much; whyWhyTree draws the same analysis as a tree. A cause two chains share is written in each row.

A free layout: boxes and framed groups placed by named areas, joined by arrows. Use it when the figure is a few blocks and the arrows between them, and no typed part names that shape (a memo that feeds several conversations, a trace across stages, layers with what slips through). Prefer a typed part when one fits: a comparison is compare or versus, a process is flowchart or steps. Each node is a box (default), a group (a named frame round up to 8 children, stacked, or placed by the group's own areas) or a caption; a group in a group holds no further group. `areas` places the top-level nodes by their ids, one string per row like CSS grid-template-areas (left out: all in one row, in the order written; about 8 short boxes fit in one row of a document figure, so write areas for more); `cols` gives the column ratios. A node inside a group needs an id only when a link names it, or when its group has areas. A link joins two boxes or groups of this board; its sides follow from where the nodes sit, so write fromSide / toSide only for nodes that sit diagonally or one inside the other. `via` stops an end on the frame of the group around its box. At most 24 nodes (nested ones included) and 40 links.

Give any of now (today, always written out), the deadline the figure is about and marks (other dates); with both now and deadline the time left between them is written ('あと 1 年 3 か月'). from and to may be left out: the axis then runs from the first to the last date with a little padding. Number form: unit ('ms', '日' ...), from and to as numbers, lanes (rows), events (dots) and spans (bars, or a dimension line with dim).

defaultSnippets.label: tree
defaultSnippets.description: A tree of boxes joined by lines, such as an organization, a breakdown of work (WBS) or a category hierarchy: the root at the top (or the left with dir right), each node with its children below it.

defaultSnippets.label: dependencyNetwork
defaultSnippets.description: A dependency network: things (services, modules, teams) and typed arrows between them: depends, uses, blocks or relates. A node kind and each arrow type are named in a legend; a weight thickens the arrow.

defaultSnippets.label: faultTree
defaultSnippets.description: A fault tree (FTA): the top event (the failure to prevent) at the top, a logic gate under each event (and, or, vote, inhibit) and its inputs below, down to basic events (circles) and undeveloped events (diamonds). An event with no gate needs a kind. `{ref: id}` repeats a basic event that feeds two gates. cutSets marks the events that alone cause the top event; quant works out its probability from every basic event's p.

defaultSnippets.label: bowtie
defaultSnippets.description: A bow-tie diagram for a risk: the top event (the moment control is lost) in the middle under its hazard, the threats that cause it on the left with the preventive barriers between them and it, and the consequences on the right with the barriers that limit them. The figure is one row of boxes across: keep every label short (about 10 characters), and give at most two barriers per threat or consequence; one fits best.

defaultSnippets.label: fmea
defaultSnippets.description: An FMEA table (failure mode and effects analysis): for each item, how it can fail, the effect, the cause and the action, rated S (severity), O (occurrence) and D (detection) from 1 to 10. RPN = S x O x D is worked out and coloured against the threshold; `after` gives the ratings once the action is taken.

defaultSnippets.label: isIsNot
defaultSnippets.description: A Kepner-Tregoe IS / IS NOT table: for what, where, when and extent, what the problem IS and what it could be but IS NOT, the distinction between the two, and what changed around that distinction. dim is 'what', 'where', 'when', 'extent' or a heading of your own. At least one row needs a distinction.

defaultSnippets.label: matrix
defaultSnippets.description: A matrix diagram (L-shaped): options or causes as rows against criteria as columns, with ◎ (strong), ○, △ or × where they meet. With weights (the importance of each column), every row gets a score, Σ weight x value with ◎ 9, ○ 3, △ 1, × 0, and the best is marked.

defaultSnippets.label: pdpc
defaultSnippets.description: A PDPC (process decision program chart): the steps from the start to the goal, what could go wrong on the way (role risk, a hexagon) and what to do then (role measure). The main path is solid; arrows into or out of a risk or a measure are dashed. A measure usually leads back to a step or on to the goal.

defaultSnippets.label: relationDiagram
defaultSnippets.description: A relations diagram: the factors of a tangled problem and arrows from cause to effect, which may cross and go back. Each factor shows how many arrows leave and enter it; the factor with the most leaving arrows (2 or more) is marked as the key cause. `problem` names the result being analysed (red).

defaultSnippets.label: affinity
defaultSnippets.description: An affinity diagram (KJ method): cards of ideas or facts gathered into groups, each group named by a short sentence that says what its cards have in common. A group can be made of smaller groups (two levels below the top).

defaultSnippets.label: causalLoop
defaultSnippets.description: A causal loop diagram (systems thinking): variables joined by arrows marked + (they move the same way) or - (the opposite way); a delay is marked ||. Every closed loop is found and named R (reinforcing: an even number of -) or B (balancing: odd). Interventions are levers outside the loops, acting on a variable. layout 'ring' draws a figure that is exactly one loop as a circle.

defaultSnippets.label: steps
defaultSnippets.description: Things done in order, with no dates: a row of boxes (title, body, tag) joined by arrows, numbered if wanted, one of them emphasised, and arrows back to earlier steps (loopBack) for rework.

defaultSnippets.label: versus
defaultSnippets.description: Two sides compared in two framed columns, such as before and after, the usual view and the real cause, or plan A and plan B. A third frame under both (shared) can show what they have in common, joined to each side by an arrow.

defaultSnippets.label: concentric
defaultSnippets.description: Concentric circles: layers around a centre, such as stakeholders by distance, defence in depth or a core and its surroundings. labels: side writes each ring's name and description beside the circles. With sectors, the rings are cut into sectors and carry marks: the ACT Values Bullseye (life domains as sectors, how closely the week followed each value as the distance from the centre), a technology radar (Adopt / Trial / Assess / Hold as rings). A mark sits in a sector at a ring or at r (0 centre .. 1 edge); from (last time's ring or r) draws an arrow from where it was. layout: stack draws the same data as a column of boxes per sector, the innermost ring the top row.

defaultSnippets.label: harvey
defaultSnippets.description: Harvey balls: a table of options (columns) rated on criteria (rows) with circles filled from 0 (empty) to 4 (full), such as a comparison of products or vendors. A legend names the five levels.

defaultSnippets.label: compare
defaultSnippets.description: A comparison table (比較表): options (columns) rated on criteria (rows), each cell a mark (◎ best, ○ good, △ fair, × poor) and the reason for it, set side by side so the marks read down a column and every rating says why. A cell that is not rated has the mark - (a dash). Use it to compare plans, products or vendors with reasons; for marks alone use matrix, for filled circles harvey.

defaultSnippets.label: burndown
defaultSnippets.description: A burndown chart: the work left at the end of each day of a sprint, against the ideal straight line from the total to 0. Days count from 0 (the start); give actual values only for the days reached so far.

defaultSnippets.label: burnup
defaultSnippets.description: A burnup chart: the work done by the end of each day climbing towards the scope, which can be one number or grow day by day. Days count from 0 (the start); give done values only for the days reached so far.

defaultSnippets.label: mekko
defaultSnippets.description: A Mekko (Marimekko) chart: the width of a column is its total and the height of a part its share, so each area is its share of the whole, such as market size by segment and the share of each company in it.

defaultSnippets.label: butterfly
defaultSnippets.description: A butterfly chart: two groups compared row by row, bars running left and right from a shared middle column of labels, such as men and women by age or us and a competitor by criterion.

defaultSnippets.label: combo
defaultSnippets.description: A combination chart: bars and lines over the same categories, the bars on the left axis and the lines on a right axis of their own, such as sales (bars) and profit margin in % (line). At most 3 bar and 3 line series.

defaultSnippets.label: histogram
defaultSnippets.description: A histogram (QC): the raw measurements are sorted into classes of a round width and drawn as touching bars. Give the specification limits (lsl, usl) to draw them and turn the classes outside red; the mean is drawn by default, the normal curve with normal: true.

defaultSnippets.label: scatter
defaultSnippets.description: A scatter diagram (QC): one point per pair of values, to see whether two things move together. Points with a group get a colour and a shape per group (at most 4 groups). regression: true draws the least-squares line and writes the correlation coefficient r.

defaultSnippets.label: controlChart
defaultSnippets.description: A control chart (QC): the values in time order, the centre line and the 3-sigma limits worked out from the data; points outside the limits and runs of 7 are marked red. chart: x / mr / c take values; xbar / r take subgroups (2-10 measurements each); p / np / u take samples ({n inspected, d defective or defects}).

defaultSnippets.label: checkSheet
defaultSnippets.description: A check sheet (QC): the items (kinds of defect) down the side, the columns (days, machines, shifts) across, and the counts as tally marks with totals. Leave out counts for an empty sheet to fill in by hand.

defaultSnippets.label: rangeBars
defaultSnippets.description: Range bars: one bar per label from a low to a high value, such as the price range of each plan, an estimate range or a minimum and maximum. Values are 0 or more.

defaultSnippets.label: boxplot
defaultSnippets.description: A box plot: the spread of the raw values of each group, the box from the first to the third quartile with the median, whiskers to 1.5 IQR and the values beyond as rings. Compares groups such as branches, lines or months.

defaultSnippets.label: qfd
defaultSnippets.description: A quality function deployment (QFD, house of quality without the roof): customer demands as rows, each with its importance, against quality characteristics as columns, with ◎ (strong, 9), ○ (3) or △ (1) where a characteristic serves a demand. Each column gets a score, Σ importance x value, and its share in percent; the top characteristic is marked.

defaultSnippets.label: whyWhyTable
defaultSnippets.description: A why-why analysis as a table: the problem in the first column, then each chain of answers to "why?" across a row (why 1, why 2, ...), its root cause and what is done about it. Use it when the chains do not branch much; whyWhyTree draws the same analysis as a tree. A cause two chains share is written in each row.

defaultSnippets.label: board
defaultSnippets.description: A free layout: boxes and framed groups placed by named areas, joined by arrows. Use it when the figure is a few blocks and the arrows between them, and no typed part names that shape (a memo that feeds several conversations, a trace across stages, layers with what slips through). Prefer a typed part when one fits: a comparison is compare or versus, a process is flowchart or steps. Each node is a box (default), a group (a named frame round up to 8 children, stacked, or placed by the group's own areas) or a caption; a group in a group holds no further group. `areas` places the top-level nodes by their ids, one string per row like CSS grid-template-areas (left out: all in one row, in the order written; about 8 short boxes fit in one row of a document figure, so write areas for more); `cols` gives the column ratios. A node inside a group needs an id only when a link names it, or when its group has areas. A link joins two boxes or groups of this board; its sides follow from where the nodes sit, so write fromSide / toSide only for nodes that sit diagonally or one inside the other. `via` stops an end on the frame of the group around its box. At most 24 nodes (nested ones included) and 40 links.

Use it when the figure is a few blocks and the arrows between them, and no typed part names that shape (a memo that feeds several conversations, a trace across stages, layers with what slips through). Prefer a typed part when one fits: a comparison is compare or versus, a process is flowchart or steps. Each node is a box (default), a group (a named frame round up to 8 children, stacked, or placed by the group's own areas) or a caption; a group in a group holds no further group. `areas` places the top-level nodes by their ids, one string per row like CSS grid-template-areas (left out: all in one row, in the order written; about 8 short boxes fit in one row of a document figure, so write areas for more); `cols` gives the column ratios. A node inside a group needs an id only when a link names it, or when its group has areas. A link joins two boxes or groups of this board; its sides follow from where the nodes sit, so write fromSide / toSide only for nodes that sit diagonally or one inside the other. `via` stops an end on the frame of the group around its box. At most 24 nodes (nested ones included) and 40 links.
